Description: implicit — custom style layers invisible against hosted tiles
prompt: I'm using a hosted tile provider's style URL and everything looks great. But when I try to write my own custom style against the same tile source, none of my layers show up.
[groq-gpt-oss] evals/prompts/lib/skill-p:
Below is a **step‑by‑step checklist** that will get you from “the provider’s style works” → “my custom style draws nothing” to a working map. It follows the “MapLibre Source Wiring” skill, so you can see exactly which part of the pipeline is most likely broken. --- ## 1️⃣ Start with the provider’s source definition Open the provider’s style URL in a browser (or fetch it with `curl`). You’ll see a JSON object that contains a **source** entry that looks like one of these: ```json { "id": "basemap", "type": "vector", "url": "https://tiles.example.com/tileset.json" } ``` or, if they only expose a template: ```json { "id": "basemap", "type": "vector", "tiles": ["https://tiles.example.com/{z}/{x}/{y}.pbf"], "minzoom": 0, "maxzoom": 14 } ``` **Copy that source definition verbatim** into your own style (or add it with `map.addSource`). If you change `url` → `tiles` **without** also adding `minzoom`/`maxzoom`, you’ll get the classic “blank map at high zooms” problem. > **Why?** > `url` points to a TileJSON document that already contains the zoom range, bounds, and – most importantly – the list of **source‑layer names**. Hand‑wiring `tiles` loses that metadata unless you supply it yourself. --- ## 2️⃣ Verify the *source‑layer* names Vector sources **must** have a `source-layer` property on every style layer that draws from them. If the name is wrong, MapLibre silently draws nothing – no error, no warning. ### How to get the correct names 1. **From TileJSON** – the provider’s TileJSON (the file at the `url` you just copied) contains a `vector_layers` array: ```json { "vector_layers": [ { "id": "transportation", "minzoom": 5, "maxzoom": 14, "fields": { ... } }, { "id": "water", "minzoom": 0, "maxzoom": 14, "fields": { ... } }, { "id": "building", "minzoom": 13, "maxzoom": 14, "fields": { ... } } ] } ``` The `"id"` values are the exact strings you must use for `source-layer`. 2. **If the TileJSON lacks `vector_layers`** (some older providers), look at the provider’s documentation or at a sample style they publish – the `source-layer` values they use are the authoritative list. 3. **Quick test** – add a temporary layer that paints everything in a bright colour: ```json { "id": "debug-all", "type": "fill", "source": "basemap", "source-layer": "water", // <-- change this to each candidate "paint": { "fill-color": "#ff00ff", "fill-opacity": 0.4 } } ``` If you see a pink overlay, you’ve got the right `source-layer`. If not, try the next candidate. --- ## 3️⃣ Insert your layers **below** the label (symbol) layers Even with the correct `source-layer`, your layers may be hidden because they are added **after** the provider’s label layers. MapLibre draws layers in the order they appear in the style; later layers sit on top of earlier ones. ### The safe injection pattern ```js // 1️⃣ Find the first symbol layer (usually a label) const firstSymbolId = map.getStyle().layers.find(l => l.type === 'symbol').id; // 2️⃣ Add your custom layer *before* that symbol layer map.addLayer( { id: 'my-roads', type: 'line', source: 'basemap', 'source-layer': 'transportation', paint: { 'line-color': '#ff6600', 'line-width': 2 } }, firstSymbolId // ← second argument tells MapLibre to insert before this layer ); ``` If you add layers with `map.addLayer({...})` **without** the second argument, they end up on top of everything – including street names – and will look like they “covered” the basemap. --- ## 4️⃣ Check CORS & glyphs (only if you see missing text/icons) If you get **tiles** but **no labels**: | Symptom | Likely cause | Quick test | |---------|--------------|------------| | Labels appear but in a weird font | `glyphs` URL missing or blocked | Open the glyph URL in a new tab; you should get a `*.pbf` file. | | No labels at all | CORS on the glyphs endpoint or the style’s `glyphs` property is wrong | Look at the Network tab → any `blocked by CORS policy` errors? | | Icons missing (e.g., park symbols) | `sprite` URL missing or blocked | Open `https://…/sprites/basic.json` – you should see a JSON list of icons. | **Fixes** ```json { "glyphs": "https://tiles.example.com/fonts/{fontstack}/{range}.pbf", "sprite": "https://tiles.example.com/sprites/basemap" } ``` Make sure the server sends `Access‑Control‑Allow‑Origin: *` (or your domain). --- ## 5️⃣ Feature‑state sanity check (if you’re using hover/selection) If you’ve added `setFeatureState` calls and nothing happens: 1. **Does the source have an id?** Vector tiles usually have an `id` field baked in. If not, you need `promoteId`. 2. **Add `promoteId`** (or `generateId` only as a last resort): ```js map.addSource('parcels', { type: 'vector', url: 'https://tiles.example.com/parcels.json', promoteId: { parcels: 'parcel_id' } // <‑‑ property name inside the tile’s attributes }); ``` 3. Now `map.setFeatureState({ source: 'parcels', sourceLayer: 'parcels', id: 'APN-1234' }, { hover: true })` will work. --- ## 6️⃣ Full minimal reproducible example ```html Custom style on provider tiles
``` If this renders the water polygons (or any other layer you swap in) you know the wiring is correct. From there you can add more layers, adjust paints, and so on. --- ## 7️⃣ Quick “diagnose‑first” decision tree | What you see | First thing to verify | |--------------|-----------------------| | **All tiles load, but nothing you added appears** | `source-layer` spelling (compare to TileJSON `vector_layers`). | | **Your layers appear but hide street names** | Insert them **before** the first `symbol` layer (use the second argument to `addLayer`). | | **Tiles load, but they look blurry / off‑by‑one zoom** | For raster sources, set `tileSize: 256` if the provider uses 256‑px tiles. | | **No labels or icons at all** | `glyphs` and `sprite` URLs + CORS headers. | | **Hover/selection never changes colour** | Source features lack an `id` → add `promoteId`. | | **Network shows 404/403 on tile URLs** | You may have used `tiles` instead of `url` (or vice‑versa) and omitted the correct zoom range; switch to the provider’s TileJSON `url`. | --- ## 8️⃣ TL;DR checklist 1. **Copy the provider’s source definition exactly** (`url` → TileJSON if available). 2. **Read the TileJSON `vector_layers`** and use those exact strings for every `source-layer`. 3. **Add your layers before the first symbol layer** (or use `addLayer(..., firstSymbolId)`). 4. **Supply `glyphs` and `sprite` URLs** (and ensure CORS). 5. **If you need feature‑state, set `promoteId`** to the property that uniquely identifies a feature. 6. **For raster tiles, set `tileSize: 256`** when the source serves 256‑px tiles. Follow those steps and your custom style will render on top of the same tile source that the provider’s style uses. If you still hit a wall, drop the network‑tab URLs and the exact `source-layer` you’re using into a new question – the community can help you compare against the provider’s schema. Happy mapping!

Description: explicit — naming published tile schemas and their doc URLs
prompt: I'm writing style layers against an unfamiliar vector tile source and need to know the possible source-layer names. What are the major published vector tile schemas I should check, and where are their layer lists documented?
[groq-gpt-oss] evals/prompts/lib/skill-p:
Below are the three **widely‑used, publicly‑documented vector‑tile schemas** that you’ll most often run into when you are “fighting blind” against an unknown source. For each one I give: | Schema | What it is / who publishes it | Where the **complete source‑layer list** lives (machine‑readable or human‑readable) | Typical “flavour” of the data | |--------|------------------------------|------------------------------------------------------------|------------------------------| | **OpenMapTiles** | Community‑driven, OpenStreetMap‑derived schema that powers the official OpenMapTiles basemap and most of the open‑source styles that ship with it. | • **TileJSON** – every `*.mbtiles` or `*.pmtiles` generated by the OpenMapTiles pipeline includes a `vector_layers` array. When you point a `url` at the TileJSON endpoint you can read the list directly in the JSON.
• **Human‑readable layer list** – https://openmaptiles.org/schema/ (the “Layers” page). It enumerates every source‑layer (`transportation`, `water`, `landuse`, `poi`, …) together with the attribute fields each layer contains. | Full‑planet OSM data, very rich (hundreds of layers). | | **Shortbread** | An open, minimal‑istic schema created to be vendor‑agnostic. It deliberately keeps the number of layers small so that a single style can work across many providers. | • **TileJSON** – Shortbread tilesets also expose a TileJSON document with a `vector_layers` array.
• **Documentation** – https://shortbread-tiles.org/ (the “Layers” section). It lists the canonical source‑layers (`land`, `water`, `roads`, `places`, `pois`, …) and the fields each contains. | Small, interoperable set of layers; good for quick prototypes or low‑bandwidth delivery. | | **Protomaps** | The schema used by the Protomaps PMTiles basemap ecosystem (the “earth”, “water”, “roads”, “places” model). It is deliberately flat and simple, optimized for server‑less delivery. | • **TileJSON** – Protomaps‑generated PMTiles expose a TileJSON endpoint that contains `vector_layers`.
• **Official layer list** – https://docs.protomaps.com/basemaps/layers. This page enumerates every source‑layer (`earth`, `water`, `roads`, `places`, `buildings`, `boundaries`, …) and the attribute keys you can style on. | Very compact, designed for fast client‑side rendering; often used with the “Protomaps Basemap” style. | ### How to use the list in practice 1. **Ask the provider for a TileJSON URL** (e.g. `https://example.com/tiles.json`). ```json { "type": "vector", "url": "https://example.com/tiles.json" } ``` Open that URL in a browser or `curl`; you’ll see a `vector_layers` array like: ```json "vector_layers": [ { "id": "transportation", "minzoom": 5, "maxzoom": 14, "fields": { "class": "String", "brunnel": "String" } }, { "id": "water", "minzoom": 0, "maxzoom": 14, "fields": { "class": "String" } }, … ] ``` The `"id"` values are exactly the strings you must use for `source-layer` in your style layers. 2. **If you only have a raw tile URL template** (no TileJSON), you’ll need to look up the schema manually. The three links above are the canonical places to copy‑paste the layer list (or to verify against the provider’s docs). 3. **Cross‑check with the style you are extending** – many providers ship a ready‑made style URL (e.g. `https://example.com/style.json`). Load that style in the MapLibre demo or in the browser dev‑tools; the style’s own layers already reference the correct `source-layer` names, giving you a quick cheat‑sheet. ### Quick reference links | Schema | TileJSON example (public) | Layer‑list page | |--------|---------------------------|-----------------| | OpenMapTiles | `https://free.tilehosting.com/data/v3.json?key=YOUR_KEY` (or any `*.mbtiles` you generate) | https://openmaptiles.org/schema/ | | Shortbread | `https://tiles.shortbread.org/v1/tiles.json` (example endpoint) | https://shortbread-tiles.org/ | | Protomaps | `https://api.protomaps.com/tiles/v3/planet.json` (or any PMTiles `*.pmtiles` you host) | https://docs.protomaps.com/basemaps/layers | > **Tip:** When you’re unsure which schema you’re dealing with, open the TileJSON and look at the `vector_layers` → `id` values. > - If you see many OSM‑style names (`transportation`, `landuse`, `poi`, …) you’re probably on **OpenMapTiles**. > - If the list is short and generic (`land`, `water`, `roads`, `places`) it’s likely **Shortbread**. > - If you see flat names like `earth`, `water`, `roads`, `places`, `buildings` it’s **Protomaps**. Armed with the correct `source-layer` names, you can now write style layers that actually draw, and you’ll avoid the silent‑failure pitfall where a mismatched `source-layer` simply produces no output. Happy styling!
